title: Introduction
paragraphs: Chapter 1 Introduction Chapter abstract. This chapter introduces the problem: social-media radio shapes what students hear, trust, and learn, yet platform design and audience measurement are usually studied separately. It states the research questions, objectives, hypotheses, scope, and the evidence hierarchy used throughout. It explains why a measured eld wave is combined with a calibrated in-silico experiment rather than a real platform trial, and it denes the contribution: an EST-based design framework, a transparent measurement model, and a reproducible testbed. It closes with the structure of the thesis. 1.1 Background and Motivation Internet distribution and social networking connect audio production with new forms of discovery, circulation, and audience response. The scholarly question is not whether these technologies are uniformly benecial or harmful, but how specic arrangements change what people encounter and how they evaluate it (Spinelli & Dann, 2019; Sullivan, 2019). Evidence about misinformation and algorithmic selection motivates the inquiry without resolving it. Vosoughi et al. (2018) analyse true and false news 1

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 2 circulation on Twitter; their result is not a universal law governing every audio network. Gauthier et al. (2026) identify some eects of feed assignment but not uniform changes across political outcomes. These ndings support examining architecture while requiring careful outcome denitions and contextual limits. The present thesis develops Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), species the LOKLOK platform, and examines audience evaluations in a journey-related listening setting. It links a eld questionnaire to a separate calibrated simulation. The aim is a defensible account of the relationships among architecture, judgments, and measurement, rather than an assumption that a positive rating demonstrates accurate content or successful learning. 1.2 From Internet Radio to Social Media Radio Internet delivery, radio programming, on-demand access, and social networking describe dierent properties. A station can stream a linear programme without listener proles. A podcast can be downloaded without a social feed. A social network can carry an audio clip without a continuous radio service. Treating these as interchangeable would obscure the study's population and the architectural intervention it proposes. Rime et al. (2022) examine podcasting through tensions rather than a single xed technological denition. Sullivan (2019) distinguishes the storage, discovery, and consumption functions of podcast platforms. An episode may therefore be hosted in one place, discovered through a social post, and heard through another interface. Table 1.1 gives this thesis's working classication, not a universal taxonomy

Author-developed distinctions informed by Spinelli and Dann (2019), Sullivan (2019), and Rime et al. (2022). Forms can overlap; classication should follow the actual listening and distribution setting. 1.2.1 Broadcasting and Social Circulation A host can post an episode, a listener can circulate an extract, and others can comment, challenge, or recommend it. Spinelli and Dann (2019) discuss audio production and relationships with listeners in podcasting. This supports examining radio as more than a transmitterreceiver pair, but does not imply equal participation or improved information merely because interaction is possible. This thesis distinguishes editorial selection, platform selection, and listener selection. Editorial selection determines what is recorded and how claims are framed. Platform selection determines which posts become visible. Listener selection includes choosing, replaying, ignoring, and sharing. EST concerns the relationship among these stages. Assigning all three to an abstract algorithm would obscure responsibility and prevent a precise explanation of eects.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 4 1.2.2 Why Social Media Radio Matters The form brings together voice-based communication, networked circulation, and visible audience metrics. It therefore oers a setting for studying how trust in a speaker relates to trust in a message and how metrics aect visibility. Student participation can also involve questioning, sourcing, production, and correction. These are opportunities motivating the research, not ndings that the present respondents acquired those capabilities. The same aordances create risks. An extract can omit qualications in a longer programme; popularity can become a credibility cue; and a correction may reach a dierent audience from the original post. Access depends on connectivity, devices, language, and accessible interfaces. Greater technical reach is not equivalent to equitable participation, and audio convenience is not equivalent to sustained attention. Transcripts and source links could support review, but their availability and use require separate measurement. Listening context matters. Groot Kormelink et al. (2025) found that repeated news-podcast use was organised around particular everyday routines. The journey setting here is therefore a concrete reception context, not grounds for assuming that commuters are uniformly attentive or distracted. Journey duration and reported interaction remain contextual variables until listening time and attention are independently measured.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 5 1.2.3 Why a Radio-Specic Case Rather Than Generic Social Media The thesis does not claim that social media radio is a representative sample of all social media. It uses social media radio as a bounded, mechanism-oriented case in which the propositions of EST can be specied, manipulated, and measured without conating modality with architecture. The distinction is a scope condition, not a rhetorical preference. Three features make the case scientically productive. First, radio-like audio is voice-centred and temporally organised. A listener encounters a programmed stream or an episode, not an undierentiated multimodal feed. This makes broadcaster identity, vocal presence, sequence, and repair observable, and it gives engagement a behavioural referent (continued listening, replay, interaction) rather than a generic click. Second, the form combines editorial selection with platform selection and listener selection (Section 1.2). That combination allows the BRS, diversityconstrained recommendation, echo control, and correction to be varied as separate architectural levers. Third, the eld population and instrument are dened for this setting: university students listening to social media radio during a ride, rating broadcaster credibility, perceived benet, and their own media competence. The outcome semantics therefore match the stimulus. A generic social media design would weaken identication in four ways. (i) Modality and architecture would co-vary: text, image, video, short-form, live, and ranked feeds bundle dierent attention regimes, production costs, and credibility cues. (ii) Outcome measures would not be construct-equivalent: a like, a watch time, a completed listen, and a credibility rating are not interchangeable. (iii) The

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 6 treatment set would be underidentied: many platform features would change at once, so a contrast could not be attributed to the BRS, diversity, or echo control. (iv) External validity would be asserted rather than demonstrated: a nding from one platform cannot be extended to social media by relabelling the object. A radio-specic case narrows the claim and makes the conditions of transfer explicit. The logic is analytical rather than statistical generalization. LOKLOK is a plausibility probe for EST: if the specied architecture produces the predicted trade-o under controlled assignment, the theory gains support within the model; if it does not, the theory is challenged. The case is not a prevalence estimate for platforms, nor a human treatment eect. The appropriate inferential target is the mechanism, not the medium. The pipeline follows this scope logic. The eld wave xes the population and the radio-specic instruments. The qualitative stream supplies candidate design vocabulary about listening, trust, participation, and correction; it is not a calibration target. The BGE-M3 four-stream representation encodes quantitative, qualitative, stimulus, and reference material, but the embedding is a pipeline feature, not evidence of human delity. The ABM instantiates the eight cells with 500 personas and 18 sessions, varying BRS, diversity, and echo control inside a radio-like feed; the randomized-assignment triangulation then tests whether the estimated contrast depends on assignment and interference. The outcomes remain SReval, SRcomp, and engagement, which are meaningful for this case. Extending the pipeline to text, image, or video platforms would require revalidated instruments, modality-specic stimuli, and a new identication argument; it is not a relabelling exercise. Table 1.2

Audience evaluations, including stars and questionnaire scores; not academic grades or demonstrated learning outcomes. Perceived credibility. A judgment of believability or trustworthiness, distinguished from content accuracy, which requires an external assessment of the claims. Engagement. A family of behaviours or reports. A click, a completed listen, a comment, and a self-reported interaction category are not interchangeable quantities. Broadcaster score and broadcaster questionnaire. The algorithmic BRS is a design object; the 11-item broadcaster-rating battery

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 8 is an audience instrument. Reliability of the latter does not directly establish accuracy or fairness of the former. Observation. The eld analysis uses 52 retained questionnaire records. An episode, a post, a broadcaster, and a simulation run are dierent units. Their counts cannot replace the number of independent respondents. EST proposes mechanisms; LOKLOK species an architecture; the questionnaire describes audience judgments; and the simulation explores conditional contrasts. These components belong together but warrant dierent conclusions. 1.4 The Research Problem The original title, The Social Media Radio Innovation and its impact on University Students Ratings, names the research problem rather than asserting that every impact has already been causally identied. Student Rating refers to the student's media competence and development; students' ratings of broadcasts refers to audience evaluations. The eld survey measures the latter. Section 3.7 distinguishes the human competence construct from the proposed computational extension. That extension tests synthetic task performance and platform dynamics, with exploratory NMLS-format responses; it does not supply a human competence eect. The thesis addresses an integration problem identied in the reviewed literature. Accounts of broadcast authority, social trust, credibility, algorithmic curation, and constrained attention illuminate dierent parts of platform communication. EST brings them into a single proposed framework with explicit architectural

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 9 and measurement commitments. This is an argument for a particular synthesis, not proof that no earlier theory considered these relationships. The empirical problem is how to distinguish a platform's reputation design from audience judgments of that design and from independently assessed information quality. The framework must specify what is measured, which relationships are observed, and which claims require an intervention. The eld questionnaire and model comparison address dierent parts of that problem and are reported separately. 1.5 The Contribution of This Thesis This thesis makes a single integrated contribution: an original theoretical framework, Epistemic Systems Theory (EST), together with an epistemic governance platform (LOKLOK) that implements selected mechanisms and species others for prospective testing, an empirical evaluation that combines a measured eld wave with a calibrated in-silico counterfactual experiment, and an evaluated set of survey instruments. The framework is developed in Chapter 3; the platform is specied, with its historical implementation account distinguished in Chapter 4; the empirical evaluation is in Chapters 5 and 6. Four components develop and examine the framework. First, a eld measurement wave of 52 university students who listen to social-media radio while riding with Uber in the October 6th City area of Giza produced a survey battery with reported internal consistency and factor-t diagnostics (Chapter 6). Second, a calibrated two-arm in-silico experiment representing alternative platform rules esti-

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 10 mated a model-conditional contrast between an epistemic-rst and an engagementrst architecture. Third, the 60 supplied rider accounts support a thematic analysis and a 52-case paired joint display. Fourth, the LOKLOK implementation account describes a Go backend, Flutter client, and web application. Their delity to the reference equations must be established before the planned agent experiment; a scalar production score is not automatically the theoretical BRS. The four-stream BGE-M3 embedding is a pipeline feature, not the headline contribution: the source ablation later shows that the semantic block is contextual, while the contrast is carried by the mechanism and the state-outcome weights. 1.6 Research Questions The thesis retains four theory-led questions, adds two mixed-methods questions, and species a student-focused question for the extended design. These additions are not retrospectively described as preregistered. RQ1RQ4 do not map one-to-one onto its four propositions: RQ4 examines integration, whereas P4 motivates the prospective task-performance comparison in H7 and RQ7. 1. RQ1 (Structural determination). Do platform architecture, credibility metrics, and content-ranking functions determine epistemic outcomes (perceived quality, credibility, diversity) more than user-level characteristics do? 2. RQ2 (Diversity constraints). Under the specied network and ranking rules, do active diversity constraints alter concentration and engagement in the directions proposed by EST-P2? 3. RQ3 (Psychometric accountability). To what extent do the consequential

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 11 metrics of the platform, the Broadcaster Reputation Score (BRS) and the survey instruments, meet published psychometric standards? 4. RQ4 (Integration). Do the epistemic constructs of EST behave as facets of a single consolidated quality channel, both in the measured wave and in the calibrated counterfactual experiment? 5. RQ5 (Audience experience). How do the rider records describe credibility, listening value, participation, and platform experience? 6. RQ6 (Integration). Where do these accounts converge with, complement, or challenge the paired questionnaire ratings? 7. RQ7 (Computational extension). How does assigned exposure to the specied LOKLOK congurations change evidence-anchored agents' task accuracy, media production, and exposure relative to G0? If held-out human outcomes are available, how accurately do the agents reproduce them? 1.7 Research Objectives 1. Develop EST with four formal propositions from which testable hypotheses can be deduced (Chapter 3). 2. Specify and implement LOKLOK, an epistemic-rst social media radio platform (Chapter 4). 3. Integrate the eld questionnaire with a transparent thematic analysis of rider records to examine audience evaluations and measurement properties (Chapter 5). 4. Calibrate an agent-based model to the measured wave and run a specied

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 12 two-arm counterfactual experiment (Chapter 5). 5. Distinguish human Student Rating from broadcast evaluations and specify a computational extension using independent task accuracy, with NMLS-format responses as secondary synthetic diagnostics. 6. Evaluate the hypotheses and propositions and draw design and policy conclusions (Chapter 6). 1.8 Hypotheses Seven hypotheses organise the evaluation. H1 to H4 are primary in the thesis structure, not certied as prospectively registered tests; H5 and H6 are exploratory, while H7 is formulated for the prospective computational extension. Their assessment distinguishes eld associations, model results, and outcomes not directly measured. Each hypothesis is mapped to a proposition of EST. 1. H1 (Structural credibility, EST-P1). Exposure to an epistemically architected interface is positively associated with perceived credibility and condence. 2. H2 (Diversity mechanism, EST-P2). Architectural exposure increases the perceived diversity of consumed content and reduces echo-driven repetition. 3. H3 (Psychometric validity, EST-P3). The study instruments demonstrate acceptable internal consistency, while structural validity is rigorously examined rather than assumed. 4. H4 (EST integration, EST-P1 to P3). The epistemic measures form a positive manifold consistent with one consolidated quality channel.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 13 5. H5 (DeGroot conformity, EST-P2, exploratory). Correction acceptance and echo-persistence dynamics behave as conformity processes. 6. H6 (Scheduling and duration, EST-P1, exploratory). Listening persistence is architecture-dependent and trades o against perceived quality. 7. H7 (Participatory performance, EST-P4; prospective). Under matched model, content, network, and resource conditions, the specied platform support improves agent claim-appraisal accuracy and evidence-based contributions relative to the comparison conguration. Task accuracy is the primary endpoint and production quality is secondary. This computational hypothesis concerns observed outputs, not inferred human development. The prospective LLM extension is a further methodological objective, not a completed hypothesis test. It will use consent-compatible qualitative anchors to guide agents operating an isolated instance of LOKLOK, and will test synthetic task performance, exposure, and production. Any additional claim of human delity requires outcomes withheld from agent prompts; without them, inference remains computational. 1.9 What the Student Ratings Mean Student Rating is an umbrella term in this thesis, not a single number. Table 1.3 xes the meaning of each rating before the results are presented. The evaluative Student Rating (SReval) is a 17 score built from the credibility and perceived-benet items and scored through the GRM model. The competence-format Student Rating (SRcomp) is a 0100 display built from the synthetic NMLS battery. Perceived benet

A 1-point change on the 17 scale is not equivalent to a 1-point change on the 0100 scale, and neither is a human learning gain. 1.10 Scope and Delimitations The measured wave is a cross-sectional questionnaire of 52 students who listen to social media radio during rides with Uber in the October 6th City area, Giza. It is a psychometric anchor, not a completed eld experiment. The causal contrast between architectural congurations is evaluated in a calibrated in-silico experiment and is

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 15 explicitly disclosed as such. The next platform-in-the-loop extension is a proposed computational design specied in Chapter 5; a longitudinal human comparison remains a separate future study, not a prerequisite for bounded computational claims. Every claim in the results chapters is tied to the questionnaire, recorded qualitative accounts, or the historical calibrated simulation; no result is asserted on the basis of projected trajectories. 1.11 Thesis Structure Chapter 2 reviews six epistemic dimensions of social media audio in the existing literature. Chapter 3 develops EST and its four propositions. Chapter 4 species the LOKLOK platform and its reported implementation boundaries. Chapter 5 describes the mixed-methods eld study, historical calibrated model, and planned LLM platform extension. Chapter 6 reports the results. Chapter 7 draws conclusions, states limitations, and outlines the conrmatory pathway. Chapter summary. Chapter 1 sets the question and the boundaries. The thesis asks whether LOKLOK's design can improve epistemic quality without destroying engagement, but it does not claim a causal eld eect. The measured wave anchors the problem; the simulation explores design implications. The contribution is the integration of theory, measurement, and a reproducible formal model, with explicit limits on what each evidence tier can support.
